Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 34
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Navy Officer
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 33

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Crowding: Crowded places, Spatial Triggers: Physical locations, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Punishment Thinking: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened, Avoid Friends: avoid seeing friends, Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark).
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others

Vignette:
Marcus is a 34-year-old Navy officer who has spent nearly fifteen years in service, much of it at sea. He came to therapy at the urging of his wife, who had grown increasingly worried about the changes she saw in him over the past eighteen months. He agreed to come, he said, because he was tired of feeling like a ghost in his own life.

The event that changed everything occurred during a routine humanitarian mission. His ship had been deployed to provide disaster relief after a catastrophic hurricane struck a coastal region. Marcus had been part of a team sent ashore to assist with evacuations. What he encountered was not the orderly operation he had trained for. The streets were flooded, the power was out, and the air was thick with the smell of saltwater, fuel, and alcohol from a nearby distillery that had been breached. In the chaos, he had helped carry a young child through chest-deep water to a makeshift shelter. He remembered the child’s grip on his neck, the way the water pushed against his chest, the absolute darkness inside the building where they took shelter. He remembered thinking, *this is not supposed to happen to me*. Even now, the memory feels so extreme that he sometimes struggles to believe it actually happened. The images come back as vivid pictures—the black water, the child’s face, the smell—but they feel disconnected from the person he was before.

In the months that followed, Marcus found himself changing in ways he did not fully understand. He began avoiding seeing friends, even those he had served with for years. When they called, he let the phone ring. When they invited him to barbecues or gatherings, he made excuses. He told himself he did not deserve their company. A quiet, persistent thought had taken root: he deserved to suffer because of what had happened. He could not articulate why—he had done his job, he had helped—but the feeling was absolute. He began to avoid any circumstance that reminded him of the event. He stopped going out after dark. He would not walk through a room with the lights off. He asked his wife to keep the blinds open during the day, but at night he insisted on a lamp burning in every room. The darkness, even in his own home, made his body tense, as if the water were rising again.

The smells were the hardest. He could not tolerate the smell of alcohol. It did not matter if it was beer, wine, or hand sanitizer—the moment it reached his nose, his chest would tighten, and he would feel his arms lock, his neck strain, as though he were still carrying that child through the flood. He would find himself standing rigid, his hands clenched, his breathing shallow, his body reenacting a position he had not chosen. He had come to believe that the memory lived in his muscles, not just his mind.

His work as a Navy officer became a minefield. His duties required him to be on base, to move through crowded hallways and briefing rooms, to stand in formation. But crowds now felt suffocating. The press of bodies, the noise, the inability to see an exit—all of it triggered a surge of panic that he had to fight to control. He learned to stand near walls, to keep his back protected, to scan for escape routes. His commanding officer noticed he had become withdrawn, less willing to take on leadership roles. Marcus told himself he no longer belonged anywhere—not on the ship, not at home, not among his friends. He used to be a happy person, he remembered that version of himself, but that man felt like a stranger. Now he was always miserable, always watching, always waiting.

What finally brought him to seek help was a moment at home. His wife had asked him to pick up takeout. He drove to the restaurant, but when he saw the crowd inside, he could not get out of the car. He sat in the parking lot for forty-five minutes, gripping the steering wheel, his body locked in that familiar position, the smell of cooking oil and beer drifting through the vents. He drove home without the food. His wife found him in the garage, sitting in the dark car, and she did not yell. She just sat down on the floor next to the driver’s door and waited. That night, she told him she was afraid for him, and he realized he was afraid too. He came to therapy hoping to feel less like a stranger in his own skin, though he was not sure that was possible. What frightened him most was the thought that the happiness he had lost was gone forever, and that he would spend the rest of his life feeling set apart from everyone else.
